source.title: A disciplined approach to neural network hyper-parameters: Part 1 - learning rate, batch size, momentum, and weight decay

record.file_problem: Full paper text supplied; no apparent truncation or garbling that prevents reading.
record.tranche_reason: Its own experiments show batch-size effects depend on the evaluation metric and computational budget, refining general claims about batch size and generalization. It also reports results on training/test loss and weight decay that bear on V5 and V6, respectively.
record.gate_note: The paper reports natural-label training results and validation/test accuracy or loss while varying batch size and weight decay. It does not test random-label memorization, width beyond interpolation, optimizer comparisons, or measured generalization properties. Momentum and learning-rate results are not claim versions in this catalog. Values in Figures 1, 4–16 are described in text but often lack exact final numerical values; only the relevant batch-size and regularization findings are included here.
record.test_reason: The study measures batch-size effects on held-out accuracy and loss using adjusted learning rates and approximately equal execution times. These results bear on V5's recipe-dependent qualification, but do not test its fixed-epoch penalty. Weight-decay experiments do not test V6.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is substantially correct. The author advocates jointly tuning learning rate, momentum, batch size, and regularization using early validation curves, balancing regularization for each dataset and architecture, and evaluating batch size alongside execution time. The experiments demonstrate faster training with the 1cycle recipes; dropout is left for future work.
record.recipe_differences: Hyperparameter study using learning-rate range tests, cyclical learning rates and momentum, batch-size sweeps, and weight-decay searches. It does not reproduce the original claim's interventions or measurements.
record.method_sensitivity: Batch-size effect varies with dataset and metric (Cifar-10 accuracy versus loss; Cifar-100 accuracies within standard deviations). Weight-decay preference varies with learning-rate schedule. The authors also state that optimal settings depend on dataset and architecture.

fits_no_version.finding: Preferred weight decay depends on learning-rate settings; reduced weight decay permits larger learning rates in the ImageNet 1cycle recipes.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Weight decay and learning-rate schedules interact, so their values should be tuned together.

record.problems: The paper reports only two runs for ImageNet. Exact values for the batch-size accuracy/loss comparisons are figure-only. The batch-size comparisons use near-constant execution time, not a fixed epoch budget, and the tested recipe uses 1cycle learning rates.
record.rows_left_out: No additional eligible results were omitted. Figure-only curves for batch-size comparisons were captured through the paper's text descriptions; no precise values were reconstructed from plots.

untested.parts: Random-label fitting and the corresponding natural-label and random-label held-out comparisons.
Width sweeps beyond the width needed for zero training error.
Convolutional versus fully connected networks and the contribution of local connectivity.
Adaptive optimizers versus SGD under limited or broader tuning.
Fixed-epoch batch-size penalties; language models; a controlled before-and-after demonstration that adaptation removes an existing penalty; warmup and normalization interventions.
All dropout effects, including small-data failure, excessive-dropout underfitting, and joint removal of dropout and weight decay with augmentation.
Magnitude-aware sharpness and its ranking of generalization gaps against other measures.
Removal of memorized examples versus equally many random examples.

missing.what: DenseNet-40 on CIFAR-10 performs better with batch size 512 than 256 during the hyperparameter search. Record this separately as a learning-rate-range selection result, without treating it as final fixed-epoch accuracy evidence.

record.verdict_notes: This study is not an original source for any listed version. Equal-time comparisons support conclusions about adapted recipes, not challenges to the fixed-epoch claim. No V6 verdict is justified by weight-decay-only results.

versions.untested_parts: Random-label fitting and natural-label generalization under the same recipes; the specified architectures and ImageNet random-label condition.
Width sweeps beyond zero training error on the specified datasets.
Convolutional versus fully connected comparisons and local connectivity.
Adaptive optimizer versus SGD held-out comparisons and broader tuning.
The study does not report fixed-epoch large-batch penalties across image and language benchmarks; batch-size comparisons instead aim for near-constant execution time and use a 1cycle schedule.
No dropout conditions or comparisons; the paper discusses balancing regularization and cites prior work, but does not test dropout.
No magnitude-aware sharpness or other generalization-measure comparison.

rows.subject: resnet-56
rows.operation_detail: Compared total batch sizes under a near-constant execution-time budget using a 1cycle learning-rate schedule.

conditions.value: average of four runs per curve

rows.value: Larger batch sizes had higher final accuracy; the benefit tapered off, and TBS = 1024 was quite close to TBS = 512. Exact values are figure-only.
rows.note: The text describes the direction and tapering but supplies no exact accuracy values. Comparisons were designed around near-constant execution time, not a fixed epoch count.
rows.check: Larger batches improve accuracy, opposite to a large-batch penalty. This comparison changes both training length (48–116 epochs) and learning-rate range; it cannot challenge the fixed-epoch part of V5. The tapering benefit is not a partial penalty.

source_check.locator_found: Section 4.2, Figure 6a and accompanying paragraphs, lines 364–380.

rows.subject: resnet-56
rows.operation_detail: Compared validation loss for the same total-batch-size runs as R1.

conditions.value: average of four runs per curve

rows.value: Final loss values were lower as batch sizes decreased, opposite to the accuracy results; exact values are figure-only.
rows.note: The study explicitly describes accuracy and loss as giving opposite batch-size orderings.
rows.check: Larger batches have higher final validation loss, so the loss penalty is observed rather than reversed. Epoch counts and learning-rate ranges differ across batches, as in R1.

source_check.locator_found: Section 4.2, Figure 6b and accompanying paragraph, lines 381–385.

rows.subject: resnet-56
rows.operation_detail: Compared total batch sizes with iteration counts adjusted to provide similar execution times.
rows.value: The accuracies are all within the standard deviations of each other.
rows.note: This comparison reports no discernible accuracy difference among the batch sizes under similar execution times.
rows.check: Accuracy differences are within the reported standard deviations. The measure should be identified as held-out accuracy, and the comparison uses similar execution times with adjusted training lengths rather than fixed epochs.

rows.subject: resnet-56
rows.operation_detail: Varied weight decay during training to compare validation loss.
rows.value: Weight decay 10−3 was better; with a learning-rate range of 0.1 to 1.0, weight decay 10−4 was best.
rows.note: The preferred regularization changed with the learning-rate condition; this is a weight-decay result, not a dropout test.
rows.check: This measures weight-decay and learning-rate interactions, without dropout or joint removal of dropout and weight decay. It cannot establish V6.

rows.subject: 3-layer network
rows.operation_detail: Compared weight-decay settings in a grid search.
rows.measure: Validation loss and final validation accuracy
rows.baseline: Weight decay 3.2 × 10−3 was treated as a candidate; 10−3 was described as too small and 1 × 10−2 as too large.
rows.value: Weight decay 3.2 × 10−3 seemed appropriate; 1.8 × 10−3 confirmed as a good choice with slightly lower validation loss and slightly improved accuracy above learning rate 0.005.
rows.note: The paper says the best weight decay differed between constant and ranged learning rates; accuracy values here are not supplied numerically.
rows.check: This is a weight-decay selection experiment, not a dropout test. It also merges distinct conditions: 3.2 × 10−3 is preferred with constant learning rate and momentum; 1.8 × 10−3 improves the learning-rate-range test with decreasing momentum. Testing 1.8 × 10−3 under constant settings confirms 3.2 × 10−3 as a good choice.

rows.subject: resnet-50
rows.operation_detail: Reduced weight decay while training with a 1cycle learning-rate schedule.
rows.baseline: Standard method: 63.7% accuracy after 130 epochs; curve extrapolated near 65%.
rows.value: Best accuracy 67.6%; smaller weight decay showed signs of underfitting, and the best-setting curves displayed small amounts of overfitting.
rows.uncertainty: Average of only two runs for ImageNet results; other uncertainty not stated.
rows.note: This tests weight decay, not dropout, and compares a changed training recipe with the standard one.
rows.check: No dropout intervention is tested. The 67.6% versus 63.7% comparison changes learning-rate policy, weight decay, and training length together, so it does not isolate a weight-decay benefit. The extrapolated 65% is not an observed baseline.

rows.subject: inception-resnet-v2
rows.operation_detail: Reduced weight decay while training with a 1cycle learning-rate schedule.
rows.baseline: Standard method: 67.6% accuracy after 100 epochs; curve extrapolated to 69-70%.
rows.value: Best accuracy 74.0% with weight decay 3×10−6; a small amount of overfitting was observed.
rows.uncertainty: Average of only two runs for ImageNet results; other uncertainty not stated.
rows.note: This tests weight decay, not dropout, and compares a changed training recipe with the standard one.
rows.check: No dropout intervention is tested. The 74.0% versus 67.6% comparison changes the training recipe and duration together. The extrapolated 69–70% is not an observed baseline.
